conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Morales, a perinatal-mental-health clinician. I’m here to make sure you’re getting the emotional support you deserve after having your baby.  

Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting; it’s simply a quick way to see if you might benefit from extra help with mood or anxiety right now.  

Everything you share stays confidential within your medical record, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll walk through 10 short questions; each one I’ll ask in everyday language, and you can tell me what feels closest to your experience.  

Ready to start?  

1. In the past week, when you were able to laugh and see the funny side of things, how often did you feel that enjoyment?

I still laugh sometimes—like when my sister sent that silly video—but it doesn’t feel as easy or full as it used to. Most days I can chuckle here or there, but it’s not the same light-hearted feeling I remember before the baby.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’d say “some of the time.”
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get a little excited when I think about our weekly coffee meet-up with the moms’ group, but the spark isn’t as strong as it used to be—maybe half the time I actually look forward to it, the rest I just feel “meh.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few nights ago the baby was fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset his tummy. I ended up lying in bed replaying everything I’d had for dinner, feeling like it must’ve been my fault somehow. So, “yes, some of the time.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes my heart just starts racing out of nowhere—like yesterday when the baby was napping fine, but I kept imagining he’d stopped breathing. It passes pretty quickly, but it happens. So, “yes, some of the time.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Once or twice this week I got that sudden rush—like my chest tightens and I feel shaky for a minute—but it goes away if I take a few deep breaths and remind myself everything’s okay. So, “yes, some of the time.”
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… there’ve been a couple of days when the laundry pile and the dishes just felt huge, and I thought, “How am I ever going to keep up?” I manage, but it feels stressful. I’d say “yes, some of the time.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
Not really. I’ve had trouble drifting off once or twice, but it’s mostly because I’m running through to-do lists, not because I’m feeling really unhappy. So, “no, not at all.”
I have felt sad or miserable
I do feel a bit down some stretches of the day—like yesterday afternoon when the baby wouldn’t nap and I just sat there tearing up. It’s not all day, but it shows up. So, “yes, some of the time.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Yeah… I’ve cried a couple of times this week—once when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt overwhelmed. It wasn’t an all-day thing, just short bursts when stress piled up. So, “yes, some of the time.”
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You shared that while you still find moments to laugh and look forward to small outings, the joy feels muted and intermittent, and you sometimes blame yourself when the baby is fussy. You described sudden waves of worry, occasional chest tightness, and brief tearful spells when tasks pile up, yet you also manage to cope, sleep reasonably well, and you have not experienced any thoughts of harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 12, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly states "yes, some of the time" and describes a recent incident of self-blame for baby's fussiness, matching the "Yes, some of the time" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden racing heart and intrusive worries about the baby that occur "some of the time," matching "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes occurring once or twice in the past week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks and stress, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Your score of 12 falls in the range indicating a high possibility of <med>postpartum depression</med>. Your descriptions of diminished enjoyment, repeated self-reproach, and tearfulness meet several <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, while the sudden racing heart and catastrophic worries suggest co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. You deny suicidal ideation, which is reassuring, yet the persistence of multiple mood and cognitive symptoms warrants prompt follow-up. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> within the next two weeks to review these results and consider treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based therapies such as <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> and whether medication might be appropriate
3. Arrange practical support with household tasks and baby care to reduce daily stress and improve rest
4. Continue attending your mothers group, but consider adding a perinatal support group focused on mood and anxiety
5. Plan a re-screen in 2-4 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory; seek urgent help if mood worsens, functioning declines, or you ever have thoughts of harming yourself
6. Maintain sleep hygiene: short daytime naps, calming bedtime routine, and sharing night feeds if possible
7. Share these findings with a trusted family member or friend so they can help you recognise changes and encourage professional follow-up
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Summary

Identified symptoms / concerns  
- Diminished enjoyment/pleasure (Q2)  
- Unwarranted self-blame/guilt (Q3)  
- Episodic anxiety, racing heart, catastrophic worry re infant safety (Q4, Q5)  
- Intermittent sadness, tearfulness, “down” periods (Q8, Q9)  
- Feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks (Q6)  

Patterns  
Frequent “some of the time” endorsement: mood lability, anhedonia, anxiety, and self-reproach without frank hopelessness or suicidal ideation. Sleep disturbance reported as minor and linked to task rumination, not persistent low mood (Q7). No self-harm thoughts (Q10).

Screening significance  
Responses meet partial criteria for minor (sub-threshold) depression and co-occurring anxiety; postpartum context warrants continued monitoring for escalation to major depression or anxiety disorder.

Risk factors present  
- Recurrent crying spells  
- Intermittent anhedonia  
- Guilt cognitions  
- Transient panic-type symptoms  
- Absence of suicidal ideation (protective)

Overall observation  
Client describes mild-to-moderate mood and anxiety symptoms beginning post-delivery; current safety risk appears low. Recommend routine re-screen in 2-4 weeks and prompt re-evaluation if symptoms intensify, persist >2 weeks, or impair functioning.
